steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has been one of the main drivers of the modern developments in artificial intelligence. The engineers who brought about this A.I. revolution have come up with a vast array of heuristics that get the neural net to perform “human like” tasks. Mathematically, most of these successes can be seen as solving the function optimization/“risk minimization” question, \min_{n\in{\mathcal{N}}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{z}}\in{\mathcal{D}}}[{\rm\ell}(n,{\bm{z}})] where the members of {\mathcal{N}} are continuous functions that neural nets can represent and \ell:{\mathcal{N}}\times{\rm Support}({\mathcal{D}})\rightarrow[0,\infty) is called a “loss function”, and the algorithm only has sample access to the distribution {\mathcal{D}}. The neural experiments that succeed seem to suggest that there are many choices of \ell,~{\mathcal{N}}~\&~{\mathcal{D}} for which very accurate solutions to this question can be found easily, even though the question looks extremely difficult. This is a profound mathematical mystery of our times.

This work is about understanding better some of the most common methods of training nets. In particular we show how regularization can help the analysis and help to prove convergence to global minima for stochastic gradient methods for neural nets, in parameter regimes that are realistic and were not explored before.

In the last few years there has been a lot of new literature on provable training of different kinds of neural nets, in certain regimes of their widths or depths, or for data with very specific structure, like noisily realizable labels. Because there are so many experimental studies, it has often been surmised that Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) on neural net losses, with proper initialization and learning rate, converges to a low-complexity solution that generalizes, when such a solution exists.

But as far as we know, there is still no convergence result for any stochastic training algorithm applied to the logistic loss for even depth 2 nets (one layer of activations with any kind of non-linearity) that does not make an assumption on the width or on the data. And this is the most common way to train classifiers on binary class labelled data.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has been one of the main drivers of the modern developments in artificial intelligence. The engineers who brought about this A.I. revolution have come up with a vast array of heuristics that get the neural net to perform “human like” tasks. Mathematically, most of these successes can be seen as solving the function optimization/“risk minimization” question, \min_{n\in{\mathcal{N}}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{z}}\in{\mathcal{D}}}[{\rm\ell}(n,{\bm{z}})] where the members of {\mathcal{N}} are continuous functions that neural nets can represent and \ell:{\mathcal{N}}\times{\rm Support}({\mathcal{D}})\rightarrow[0,\infty) is called a “loss function”, and the algorithm only has sample access to the distribution {\mathcal{D}}. The neural experiments that succeed seem to suggest that there are many choices of \ell,~{\mathcal{N}}~\&~{\mathcal{D}} for which very accurate solutions to this question can be found easily, even though the question looks extremely difficult. This is a profound mathematical mystery of our times.

This work is about understanding better some of the most common methods of training nets. In particular we show how regularization can help the analysis and help to prove convergence to global minima for stochastic gradient methods for neural nets, in parameter regimes that are realistic and were not explored before.

In the last few years there has been a lot of new literature on provable training of different kinds of neural nets, in certain regimes of their widths or depths, or for data with very specific structure, like noisily realizable labels. Because there are so many experimental studies, it has often been surmised that Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) on neural net losses, with proper initialization and learning rate, converges to a low-complexity solution that generalizes, when such a solution exists.

But as far as we know, there is still no convergence result for any stochastic training algorithm applied to the logistic loss for even depth 2 nets (one layer of activations with any kind of non-linearity) that does not make an assumption on the width or on the data. And this is the most common way to train classifiers on binary class labelled data.

In this work we take a step towards this question in the theory of neural networks, and we do it while keeping to a standard algorithm, the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Our key message can be stated as follows,

If the initial weights are sampled from an appropriate class of distributions, then for nets with a single layer of sigmoid or tanh gates – for arbitrary data and size of the net – SGD on appropriately regularized logistic loss, while using constant steps of size {\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon), will converge in {\mathcal{O}}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) steps to weights at which the expected regularized loss would be \epsilon –close to its global minimum.

The threshold amount of regularization needed here does not depend on the width of the nets. Also, the threshold scales so that it is naturally small if the norms of the training data are small, or it can be made arbitrarily small by choosing the outer layer weights to be small. This result is possible because of a crucial observation, which we state informally in the following lemma, and which actually holds for more general nets than the theorem above covers,

It is possible to add a constant amount of Frobenius norm regularization on the weights, to the logistic loss on depth- 2 nets with activations like SoftPlus, sigmoid and tanh gates s.t with no assumptions on the data or the size of the net, the regularized loss would be a Villani function.

Our result does not need any assumptions on the data or on the neural net width, so we think it improves significantly on previous work in this direction. As far as we know, similar convergence guarantees in the existing literature need either some minimum neural net width that grows with the inverse accuracy and the training set size (NTK regime), or infinite width (Mean Field regime), or other assumptions on the data when the width is parametric (e.g. realizable data,).

Unlike all of these, we show that with appropriate \ell_{2} regularization, SGD on logistic loss on 2–layer sigmoid / tanh nets converges to the global infimum of the loss. The critical observation for the proof is that these standard losses on 2–layer nets are a “Villani function”, for a broad class of activation functions. The proof is then completed by using the relevant results in earlier work.

## Organization

Section 2 gives a literature review of existing proofs about guaranteed training of neural nets. Section 3 has our main results, in particular Lemma 3.3, which uses a special initialization of the weights to show global convergence of SGD on regularized logistic loss with \pm 1 labelled data and for gates like sigmoid and tanh. In Theorem 3.5 we also point out that for our architecture, if the SoftPlus activation is used, we can show that the underlying SDE converges in expectation to the global minimizer in linear time. Section 4 gives a brief overview of the methods in that earlier work, and more details are in Appendix D. In Section 3.2 we discuss experiments with synthetic data, which show that there are nets trained on this loss function that have high binary classification accuracy near the critical value of the regularizer used for the proof. More experiments with MNIST that show a similar phenomenon are in Appendix E. We end in Section 6 with a discussion of open questions that our work motivates. Appendices A to C contain the calculations needed for the proofs of the main theorems.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Modern developments in artificial intelligence have been significantly driven by the rise of deep-learning. The highly innovative engineers who have ushered in this A.I. revolution have developed a vast array of heuristics that get the neural net to perform “human like” tasks. Most such successes can mathematically be seen as solving the function optimization/“risk minimization” question, \min_{n\in{\mathcal{N}}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{z}}\in{\mathcal{D}}}[{\rm\ell}(n,{\bm{z}})] where members of {\mathcal{N}} are continuous functions representable by neural nets, \ell:{\mathcal{N}}\times{\rm Support}({\mathcal{D}})\rightarrow[0,\infty) is called a “loss function”, and the algorithm only has sample access to the distribution {\mathcal{D}}. The successful neural experiments suggest that there are many available choices of \ell,~{\mathcal{N}}~\&~{\mathcal{D}} for which highly accurate solutions to this seemingly extremely difficult question can be easily found. This is a profound mathematical mystery of our times.

This work is about developing our understanding of some of the most ubiquitous methods of training nets. In particular, we shed light on how regularization can aid the analysis and help prove convergence to global minima for stochastic gradient methods for neural nets in hitherto unexplored and realistic parameter regimes.

In the last few years, there has been a surge in the literature on provable training of various kinds of neural nets in certain regimes of their widths or depths, or for very specifically structured data, like noisily realizable labels. Motivated by the abundance of experimental studies, it has often been surmised that Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) on neural net losses – with proper initialization and learning rate – converges to a low–complexity solution that generalizes, when it exists [1].

But, to the best of our knowledge, a convergence result for any stochastic training algorithm applied to the logistic loss for even depth 2 nets (one layer of activations with any kind of non–linearity), without an assumption on either the width or the data, has remained elusive so far. We recall that this is the most common way to train classifiers on binary class labelled data.

In this work, we take a step towards addressing the above question in the theory of neural networks, and we do so while keeping to a standard algorithm, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Our key message can be summarily stated as follows,

If the initial weights are sampled from an appropriate class of distributions, then for nets with a single layer of sigmoid or tanh gates – for arbitrary data and size of the net – SGD on appropriately regularized logistic loss, while using constant steps of size {\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon), will converge in {\mathcal{O}}(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) steps to weights at which the expected regularized loss would be \epsilon –close to its global minimum.

We note that the threshold amount of regularization needed above is independent of the width of the nets. Further, this threshold scales such that it either turns out to be proportionately small if the norms of the training data are small, or can be made arbitrarily small by choosing small outer layer weights. Our result is made possible by a crucial observation informally stated in the following lemma, which in fact holds for more general nets than those encompassed by the above theorem,

It is possible to add a constant amount of Frobenius norm regularization on the weights, to the logistic loss on depth- 2 nets with activations like SoftPlus, sigmoid and tanh gates s.t with no assumptions on the data or the size of the net, the regularized loss would be a Villani function.

Since our result does not require any assumptions on the data or the neural net width, we posit that it significantly improves on previous work in this direction. To the best of our knowledge, similar convergence guarantees in the existing literature require either some minimum neural net width – growing w.r.t. inverse accuracy and the training set size (NTK regime [2,3]), infinite width (Mean Field regime [4,5,6]) or other assumptions on the data when the width is parametric (e.g. realizable data, [7,8]).

In contrast to all these, we show that with appropriate \ell_{2} regularization, SGD on logistic loss on 2–layer sigmoid / tanh nets converges to the global infimum of the loss. Our critical observation towards this proof is that these standard losses on 2–layer nets – for a broad class of activation functions – are a “Villani function”. The proof is then completed by leveraging the relevant results in [9].

## Organization

In Section 2 we give a literature review of existing proofs about guaranteed training of neural nets. In Section 3 we present our primary results, in particular Lemma 3.3, which uses special initialization of the weights to show the global convergence of SGD on regularized logistic loss with \pm 1 labelled data and for gates like sigmoid and tanh. Additionally, in Theorem 3.5 we point out that for our architecture, if using the SoftPlus activation, we can show that the underlying SDE converges in expectation to the global minimizer in linear time. In Section 4 we give a brief overview of the methods in [9], with further details in Appendix D. In Section 3.2 we discuss experiments with synthetic data, which show that there exist nets trained on the loss function considered that have high binary classification accuracy near the critical value of the regularizer considered for the proof. Further experiments with MNIST demonstrating a similar phenomenon are given in Appendix E. We end in Section 6 with a discussion of the open questions that our work motivates. The calculations needed in the main theorems’ proofs can be found in Appendices A to C.
